items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I knew Max when she was married, Max Roach when she was married to him

ctx.x: Certainly a disservice to the music.

Yeah, it’s a disservice to the music, and you know, it’s one of those things, I’m sure many black people if they look at this tape would say well we’ve certainly had enough problems in the past and this and that. But I love a thing that Abbey Lincoln said a couple of years ago. Somebody was talking about the predominance of black players in jazz. And I think anybody that knows jazz would say that’s true. Fine. If you want to say 80%, I’m going to go real high, let’s say we’re going to make a general quote of…

descendent. You know what I mean? Hey they own opera. Wouldn’t that sound stupid? Or to say anything Leontyne Price has done. “Well it’s negated by the fact that she’s not a middle-European.” And you’re laughing because it’s so silly.

items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: watch Max Roach or watch Art Blakey. Now don’t you know a great deal of how I learned how to do this stuff was from watching those guys.

ctx.x: Yeah. Thanks a lot yo mamma! You’re so tired by now, you couldn’t care less about playing a drum solo, or a bass solo. But in those days, you know what you did do was you learned how to pace yourself. So if they did ask you to play a drum solo, quite frankly, you were able to. It was something you had to learn to do, you know. And of course I was lucky I lived in New Jersey. For ten cents I hopped on a subway, walked uptown twenty blocks, learned how to buy a Coke and nurse it for three or four hours in a corner…
Sidney, but what he had brought to Bird and Dizzy’s music he also brought to the Jimmy Ryan Band. Isn’t that a wonderful gift?
